About This Simulation

Physics. Spherical harmonics Yℓm(θ, φ) are the angular eigenfunctions of orbital angular momentum in quantum mechanics. The integer ℓ sets the overall nodal complexity, while m sets the azimuthal structure around the z-axis.

Axes. The white z-axis (vertical) is the polar/quantization axis from which θ is measured. This matches the standard QM convention where Lz eigenstates have definite m.

Visuals. In Polar Surface, the radius is proportional to |Y|. In Projection, the surface is a fixed sphere colored by Y (real: sign + magnitude emphasis; complex: hue and brightness from phase and |Y|). In Point Cloud, angular acceptance is proportional to |Y|² while radius is mapped as r ∝ |Y|. Color encodes the field: Real uses a red↔blue sign/magnitude scale, while Complex uses hue for phase arg(Y) and brightness for |Y|.

Controls: Left-drag rotate · Scroll/pinch zoom · Right-drag (or two-finger drag) pan

Guided Inquiry

1 · The angular functions

Let’s get our bearings. The spherical harmonics Yℓm(θ, φ) are the angular eigenfunctions of orbital angular momentum: ℓ fixes its magnitude and m its projection on the white z axis. The surface you see has radius |Y| in each direction, blue where Y is positive and red where it’s negative. Wherever Y vanishes, the surface pinches in to the origin — here, that’s on the equatorial plane.

2 · Zero angular momentum

Let’s start with the simplest case. A state with ℓ = 0 carries no orbital angular momentum at all. What shape do you predict for Y00?

3 · Counting the nodes

Now let’s hunt for a pattern. Nodal lines are the directions where Y vanishes and the surface pinches in. Keep m = 0 and try several values of ℓ for yourself. How many nodal lines do you think Yℓ0 has?

4 · Around the equator

Time to bring m into play. Set m = 2 at ℓ = 2, then follow the equator once around with your eye. How many times do you think the surface changes between blue and red?

5 · The reach of m

One last question. Try raising m while ℓ stays at 2. How large do you think |m| can become?

The Physics

Spherical harmonics · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim draws the spherical harmonics Yℓm(θ, φ), the angular wavefunctions of a particle with definite orbital angular momentum. Two integers, ℓ and m, choose the state, and the 3-D picture shows how the wavefunction varies with direction.

What you'll learn

  • How a function of direction becomes a 3-D surface, and what the radius and the colours stand for.
  • How ℓ and m together fix a state and what each says about the angular momentum.
  • How the node counts relate to the shape you see.
  • How the Real and Complex forms of one state differ.
One direction (θ, φ): the surface is drawn at a distance set by |Y| in that direction.

What's on screen

  • Blue: Y > 0 in Real mode. Pale grey is Y ≈ 0.
  • Red: Y < 0 in Real mode.
  • White axes: x, y and z. The vertical z axis is the polar axis that θ is measured from.
  • Legend (on the canvas): the colour scale for the current mode.
  • Quantum Numbers: the label Yℓm and the two sliders.
  • Nodal Structure: three node counts for the current state. The Guided Inquiry reveals it at card 4.
See itOpen Y10 in Polar Surface mode. Watch for: a blue lobe above and a red lobe below, meeting at the origin.

03

The surface plots |Y|, not a position

A hydrogen-like orbital factors as ψ = R(r) Yℓm(θ, φ). The sim draws only Y, which depends on direction alone, so no distance from a nucleus appears anywhere in the picture.

Y is normalised over directions (solid angle), not over r.
  • Polar Surface. In each direction the surface sits at radius 1.2 |Y| / max|Y|. Where Y = 0 it pinches to the origin. In Real mode blue is Y > 0 and red is Y < 0.
  • Projection. A sphere of fixed radius 1.5, coloured by Y. The nodes are where the colour crosses zero. There are no lobes.
  • Point Cloud. Each direction is kept with probability proportional to |Y|², so the dots crowd where |Y|² is large. Each dot is still placed at a radius proportional to |Y|.

|Y|² is a probability density per unit solid angle, and the length you see is |Y|. The lobes are a plotting choice: Projection shows the same Y without them.

Y20 cut through the z axis and drawn both ways (set ℓ = 2, m = 0). Blue is Y > 0, red is Y < 0.
See itThe same Y20 drawn as a Polar Surface, then as a Projection. Watch for: the lobes turning into a smooth sphere, with the colour changing where the surface had pinched.
04

Two integers label every state

Yℓm is a simultaneous eigenfunction of L² (the squared magnitude of the orbital angular momentum) and Lz (its component along the white z axis):

ħ is the unit of angular momentum.
  • ℓ sets the magnitude: |L| = √(ℓ(ℓ+1)) ħ.
  • m sets the z component, Lz = mħ. One full turn round z must return eimφ to itself, so m is an integer.
  • The angular-momentum algebra allows only |m| ≤ ℓ. That leaves 2ℓ+1 states for each ℓ, the values the m slider steps through.
  • ℓ = 0 has no preferred direction. Y00 = 1/√(4π) ≈ 0.282 is the same in every direction.
See itSet ℓ = 0, m = 0. Watch for: a plain sphere in one colour, with no pinch anywhere.
05

Nodes split into planes and cones

A node is a direction where Y = 0. Two factors of Y can vanish, and they give two families of node:

The three counts in the Nodal Structure panel, where the cones are labelled “Latitudinal”.
  • Planes. In Real mode the azimuthal factor cos(mφ) or sin(|m|φ) gives |m| planes through the z axis.
  • Cones. Pℓ|m|(cos θ) has ℓ−|m| zeros, each a cone about z. A cone at θ = 90° is the flat equatorial plane.
  • Sign changes. In Real mode, going once round a circle of latitude that is not itself a node, the sign changes 2|m| times. The equator is a node when ℓ−|m| is odd.
All |m| at ℓ = 3: teal rings are cones, amber rings are planes.
ℓ m

These sliders move the sim too.

See itSet ℓ = 3, m = 2 in Real mode. Watch for: eight lobes, separated by the equatorial plane and two planes through z, with the node counts reading 3, 2 and 1.
06

L is always longer than Lz

A Complex harmonic is an Lz eigenstate, so Lz = mħ is sharp. But √(ℓ(ℓ+1)) > ℓ ≥ |m|, so Lz is always shorter than |L|. In the vector-model picture, L makes an angle θL with z, where cos θL = m/√(ℓ(ℓ+1)).

The vector model at ℓ = 2: five projections, none reaching √6 ħ.
  • Even at m = ℓ = 2 the best case is 2ħ out of 2.449ħ, a tilt of 35.3°.
  • The missing length has no direction. ⟨Lx⟩ and ⟨Ly⟩ are zero, but their squares are not.
  • This is forced by [Lx, Ly] = iħLz: L² and one component can be sharp together, never all three components.
The cone is bookkeeping for these numbers, not a spinning arrow.
See itStep m from 0 to 2 at ℓ = 2, in Complex mode. Watch for: Lz rising to 2ħ in the card and never reaching |L| = 2.449ħ.
07

Real and Complex harmonics differ in Lz

Both forms have the same ℓ and the same L². They differ in what they say about Lz.

How the sim builds its Real form from the Complex harmonic.
  • Complex is the Lz eigenstate. |Y| has no φ dependence, so the surface is symmetric about z, and the φ structure appears as hue: the phase winds |m| times round each circle of latitude.
  • Real mixes +|m| and −|m| equally. It has lobes and sign changes, and ⟨Lz⟩ = 0.
  • At m = 0 the two forms are identical, because there is no eimφ factor.
  • The sim plots Y(θ, φ) only. A stationary state's time factor e−iEt/ħ is the same in every direction, so it would change no shape.
See itY22 in Real mode, then in Complex mode. Watch for: four separate lobes turning into a ring-shaped surface about z, with the colour cycling twice round it.
08

Where it matters

  • Atomic orbitals. The angular part of every hydrogen-like orbital is a Yℓm. The letters s, p, d, f stand for ℓ = 0, 1, 2, 3, and the chemist's px, py, pz are the Real forms. The radial part, which this sim does not draw, sets the size.
  • Rotating molecules. The rotational states of a rigid diatomic molecule are YJm, with energy ħ²J(J+1)/(2I) and 2J+1 states at each level.
  • The cosmic microwave background. The temperature pattern over the whole sky is expanded in spherical harmonics. A multipole ℓ corresponds roughly to an angular scale of 180°/ℓ, and the first acoustic peak sits near ℓ ≈ 220.
Go deeper: the Zeeman shift
  • A magnetic field B along z adds an orbital energy μBBm, so it picks out the Complex harmonics. With μB = 57.9 μeV/T, ℓ = 2 splits into five levels spanning 4μBB = 0.23 meV at 1 T (orbital motion only; spin adds its own shift).
  • In a crystal field, which has lower symmetry than a sphere, the energy eigenstates are usually Real combinations such as dxy and dz².
09

Summary

In one line. Yℓm is the angular wavefunction with L² = ℓ(ℓ+1)ħ² and Lz = mħ. The sim plots its size as the radius and its sign or phase as colour.

Key points

  • ℓ sets |L|, m sets Lz, and each ℓ has 2ℓ+1 values of m.
  • The angular nodes are |m| planes plus ℓ−|m| cones.
  • Lz is always shorter than |L|; the difference is spread over Lx and Ly.
  • Complex harmonics are Lz eigenstates. Real harmonics mix +|m| and −|m|.

Common mix-ups

  • "The lobes show how far the electron is from the nucleus." The radius is |Y| in that direction. Distance from the nucleus belongs to R(r), which is not drawn.
  • "Red means negative probability." Red is Y < 0 in Real mode. The probability density |Y|² is never negative.
  • "m is the angular momentum." m gives only the z component, Lz = mħ. The magnitude √(ℓ(ℓ+1)) ħ is always larger.

Things to try on your own

  • Set ℓ = 4, m = −2 in Real mode. Work out the numbers of planes and cones, then check them against the Nodal Structure panel.
  • At ℓ = 3, step m from 0 to 3 and note which values make the equator a node.
  • Switch ℓ = 3, m = 1 to Complex and count how many times the hue cycles round a circle of latitude.
